item.title: Guam Veterans Day ceremony honors service while highlighting challenges facing veterans
item.description: Guam’s 2026 annual Veterans Day observance honored generations of military service while highlighting the ongoing need for accessible health care and support for the island’s veterans. The ceremony was held Wednesday at Gov. Joseph Flores Memorial Park at Ypao Beach. The observance brought together government officials, military leaders, veterans, and community members to recognize those who serve
item.content:encoded:
Guam’s 2026 annual Veterans Day observance honored generations of military service while highlighting the ongoing need for accessible health care and support for the island’s veterans.

The ceremony was held Wednesday at Gov. Joseph Flores Memorial Park at Ypao Beach. The observance brought together government officials, military leaders, veterans, and community members to recognize those who served in the U.S. armed forces and the families who supported them.

Keynote speaker Major General Esther J.C. Aguigui (Ret.), Guam’s Homeland Security Advisor, connected the island’s military contributions to its history, particularly the experiences of CHamoru families during the Japanese occupation in World War II.

Aguigui said Guam has more than 20,000 veterans, many of whom continue to face challenges accessing health care and Department of Veterans Affairs services. She noted that some veterans must wait for speciality care or travel to Hawaii for treatment unavailable on Guam.

“An island that gives the most has too often received the least,” Aguigui said.

She also called attention to women veterans who may not identify themselves as veterans or claim the benefits they earned through their service. Aguigui encouraged women who served in the military to recognize themselves as veterans and seek the care and services available to them.

“Since 1948, when women were first allowed to serve as permanent members of our armed forces, the daughters of Guam have answered the same call as our sons,” Aguigui said.

Aguigui outlines several efforts by the Leon Guerrero-Tenorio administration to improve veterans’ services, including advocating for a VA regional office on Guam, incorporating a veterans clinic into the planned Guam Medical Complex, and relocating the Office of Veterans Affairs to a new facility in Hagåtña.

She also highlighted efforts to digitize veterans’ records, train volunteer veterans services officers, and improve the Guam Veterans Cemetery in Piti. Those improvements include repairs to existing crypts and plans to add approximately 1,480 graves through a grant from the National Cemetery Administration.

Gov. Lou Leon Guerrero also addressed the gathering, recognizing the sacrifices made by veterans and their families. She connected Guam’s history of protecting its homeland to generations of residents who have served in the military and emphasized that honoring veterans should extend beyond the annual observance.

With approximately seven and a half weeks remaining in her administration, Leon Guerrero said her administration had worked to provide veterans with services they deserve and acknowledged the incoming administration for the Office of the Governor of Guam.

“I would like to recognize the Governor-elect Tony Ada and Lieutenant Governor-elect EJ Calvo, and I am very confident that I am leaving them in their hands a good administration that serves the people of Guam and our veterans,” Leon Guerrero said. “I am very confident that their leadership and their administration will continue that service moving forward.”

The ceremony also included a moment of silence for service members who died in service and veterans who have since passed away, as well as recognition of the 2026 Veterans of the Year for their accomplishments and leadership within their respective military organizations.

item.title: Chamorro lelek launch marks historic return of Saipan-built sakman
item.description: After nearly 500 years, a Saipan-built Chamorro sakman returned to Marianas waters Saturday morning as the traditional outrigger canoe Chamorro Lelek completed its maiden voyage from Susupe to Micro Beach with hundreds of spectators gathered along the shoreline. item.content:encoded:
After nearly 500 years, a Saipan-built Chamorro sakman returned to Marianas waters Saturday morning as the traditional outrigger canoe Chamorro Lelek completed its maiden voyage from Susupe to Micro Beach with hundreds of spectators gathered along the shoreline.

Community members, cultural practitioners, traditional navigators, elected officials and government leaders joined the Marianas Visitors Authority's Seafaring Traditions Program and the Commonwealth Council for Arts and Culture in celebrating the historic launch, which organizers said marked the first time in centuries that a Chamorro sakman built on Saipan had sailed in local waters.

The vessel's arrival at Micro Beach was greeted with cheers as crew members brought the canoe ashore during the Matatpanggen I Lelik/Afaifai launching ceremony honoring the maritime traditions of the Chamorro and Refaluwasch people.

John Castro, who helped lead the project through MVA's Seafaring Traditions Program, said the launch was as much about the future as it was about the past.

"So this canoe is finished, but we're not done," Castro said. "We want to keep sailing, and most importantly, we hope to inspire the next generation so it continues on. The only way we can keep our culture alive is to keep the practice going."

Castro said the project took more than eight years to complete after builders were forced to start over when an earlier canoe, carved from a log donated from Rota, was destroyed in a fire. Funding challenges, storms and limited manpower also slowed progress.

Despite the setbacks, Castro said the team remained committed to completing the canoe. "It looks like a canoe until we try it in the water," he said. "Then we can confirm if it is. Today, it is a canoe."

Among those aboard the sakman was master navigator Antonio "Tony" Piailug, son of legendary Micronesian navigator Mau Piailug. Piailug has spent the past several months training members of the Saipan seafaring group in traditional navigation and voyaging practices.

Piailug said the launch demonstrates that indigenous seafaring traditions remain alive and relevant today.

"If they want to continue, it's up to them," Piailug said of younger generations. "We try. If they want to learn, well, it's nice. For me, it's nice."

He emphasized that traditional navigation is inseparable from cultural identity.

"What we're doing is our culture. That's our identity," Piailug said. "If you know your culture, you know where you are from."

Piailug also said the sakman is designed as a voyaging canoe capable of traveling between islands, with the group hoping to attempt a voyage to Guam next year.

For organizers, the successful voyage of Chamorro Lelek represented more than the completion of a canoe project years in the making. It marked the revival of an ancient tradition that once connected the islands of the Marianas and signaled the beginning of a new generation of canoe builders, navigators and cultural practitioners dedicated to keeping that knowledge alive.

item.title: Guam Board of Education chair wants oversight hearing on Public Health's requirements for schools
item.description: Guam Board of Education Chairperson Judith Guthertz said Monday she would like the chair of the Legislature’s Committee on Education to call an immediate oversight hearing for the Department of Public Health’s Environmental Health Division. Guthertz said she was upset because people on a radio talk show were making fun of the Education Department for installing air conditioning in school restrooms
item.content:encoded:
Guam Board of Education Chairperson Judith Guthertz said Monday she would like the chair of the Legislature’s Committee on Education to call an immediate oversight hearing for the Department of Public Health’s Environmental Health Division.

Guthertz said she was upset because people on a radio talk show were making fun of the Education Department for installing air conditioning in school restrooms, but the department is merely complying with Public Health regulations.

She said the oversight hearing should be called, “with the goal of determining whether or not these regulations make sense. That is the source of many of the difficulties that we have experienced over the last few months.”

The Tiyan High School campus, which also housed students from Simon Sanchez High School, was closed by Public Health shortly after the school year began in August, leading to double sessions and emergency repairs.

She wanted the public to know the idea for cooler bathrooms did not come from the Education Department.

“People in the community don't understand this, that we have to honor those regulations, no matter whether or not they make sense,” she said, questioning whether air conditioning in restrooms would affect student learning. “I take great exception to the lack of clarification on the part of the media that do not understand where these regulations come from.”

She said air conditioning is also being installed at University of Guam restrooms.

“Can you imagine what the costs are going to be for DOE? We have to do this in every school, in every bathroom, and at the university and at GCC. Why could we not put ceiling fans? Would that not help?” she asked. “Split units, the cost of retrofitting the electrical requirements, the installation costs, the material costs, the equipment costs. I'd rather use that money in the classrooms.”

Because the matter could not be addressed during Monday’s emergency meeting for the department’s spending plan, Guthertz asked that it be placed on the board agenda for the upcoming Nov. 17 meeting.

The board will consider whether to ask the superintendent to request an oversight hearing on the Public Health requirements.

item.title: Actor Stacy Keach, who played a private eye and plenty more, dies at 85
item.description: He played outlaw Frank James in the Western The Long Riders , the bumbling Sgt. Stedenko in the Cheech and Chong stoner comedy Up in Smoke, and Hamlet on stage multiple times. item.content:encoded:
He played outlaw Frank James in the Western The Long Riders , the bumbling Sgt. Stedenko in the Cheech and Chong stoner comedy Up in Smoke, and Hamlet on stage multiple times. He narrated numerous documentaries for National Geographic and PBS.

Keach died on Tuesday at his family's home in Poland "after a long and difficult battle with a serious heart condition and heart failure," his wife Malgosia Keach shared in a statement through a representative. He was 85.

Keach seemed to be anything you wanted him to be: Born in Savannah, Ga., in 1941, he grew up in Southern California. He was classically trained at the Yale School of Drama and studied on a Fulbright scholarship at the London Academy of Music and Dramatic Art, but he was best known for playing, well, badasses: cops, cowboys, detectives — the strong, but not silent type.

In the 1980s and '90s, his fedora and signature mustache (which covered a scar from cleft palate operations as a child) served him well in his role as Mike Hammer, private eye — a character created by crime novelist Mickey Spillane.

He had a steady career except in 1984, when he was arrested at Heathrow Airport for bringing cocaine into Britain on a flight. He served six months in prison, which, he said, gave his subsequent roles more depth.

"Anybody who has an experience like that certainly carries it with them," he told NPR's Scott Simon in 1986. "And from an artistic point of view, utilizes it — or hopefully utilizes it — in a way that's going to be positive and productive. I think that the most important thing from my point of view was not taking freedom for granted."

Keach got back to work and kept acting as he got older. He did network sitcoms — playing the father of a helicopter traffic reporter along for the ride in NBC's Crowded as well as prestige films, such as Alexander Payne's Nebraska in 2013.

His first love, though, was the stage, especially Shakespeare, and anyone who saw him on stage remembered it. He said his toughest role was Macbeth: "Of all the major tragic roles in the canon, it's probably the most difficult," he told NPR's Robert Siegel in the midst of a 1995 production at the Shakespeare Theatre in Washington, D.C.

Macbeth has "a moral blindness, a blind spot in his character," that makes it a particularly interesting role, Keach explained. Shakespeare gave Macbeth the ability to put "extraordinary insights into the human condition" into poetry.

It was just one of many challenging roles Stacy Keach would take on, in a career that spanned more than half a century, on stage and on screen.

item.title: Following big Democratic wins, these swing voters are looking for results
item.description: Updated November 12, 2026 at 12:19 AM ChST Republicans were dealt a stunning rebuke in last week's midterms. But swing voters, who could be decisive in the next election, are more interested in results than investigations or impeachment as Democrats prepare to take power in Congress.
item.content:encoded:
Updated November 12, 2026 at 12:19 AM ChST

Republicans were dealt a stunning rebuke in last week's midterms. But swing voters, who could be decisive in the next election, are more interested in results than investigations or impeachment as Democrats prepare to take power in Congress.

"I am hoping that we don't experience a bunch of gridlock and a lot of whining and crying and just political infighting for the next two years," said Theresa, a voter from Pennsylvania who is participating in NPR's Swing Shift project. "I'm hoping we don't have that. I fear that we will have that."

NPR has agreed not to use the full names of the Swing Shift voters, so they can speak freely about politics without fear of personal or professional repercussions.

Theresa voted for President Biden in 2020, President Trump in 2024 and split her ticket in this year's midterms. Like many voters, her top issue this year was affordability. In a voice memo sent to NPR days after the midterms, Theresa said she is eager for the cost of living to come down.

"I just don't remember it ever being as bad in our time," Theresa said. "And I'm just hoping we get some relief and we get some relief soon."

At 9:56 PM on election night, Wally in Georgia hit send on his voice memo. He had seen enough.

"Just checking in here with a quick note. I'm not surprised at all by the outcome tonight," Wally said. "I believe that this is a lot of Trump's doing and pushback on his style of politics and how he governs."

Wally voted for Trump in 2024 but swung back to Democrats in this year's midterms. He had initially supported Trump in hopes that a Trump presidency would shake up the political system, but that didn't happen and now he says the second Trump term has been exhausting. As he sees it, the decisive Democratic wins signal that the country is ready to move on.

"Trump has been shooting himself in the foot for many months now," Wally said. "But voting isn't the end of the game here. We have to hold Democrats to some sort of tangible change and not just promises about what they want to do."

For several of the Swing Shift voters, Tuesday's results came as a surprise.

Jason from North Carolina split his ticket, voting for Democrat Roy Cooper for Senate and the Republican incumbent for the House.

"My congressman was defeated this time by someone that no one's really ever heard of," said Jason, sounding almost puzzled by the blue wave that crashed on North Carolina.

That happened in a lot of places. Jason wants the incoming Democratic Congress to focus on the cost of living and steer clear of impeachment.

"My fear is that the Democrats now are going to spend the next 2 years not focusing on any of the things that they say Trump didn't do," said Jason.

Michelle in Michigan, voted for President Biden in 2020 but chose Republicans in 2024 and again in this year's midterms.

"This is the first time I think ever since I've been voting that not one of the people that I voted for won their election," Michelle said.

Michelle says she understands why so many people voted for Democrats, even if she didn't. Americans are tired, she said, of high gas prices, the cost of living and not being able to afford their groceries. They voted for change.

John from Pennsylvania said it felt like his state went from purple to blue overnight.

"I'm just very surprised," John said. "Not surprised that Democrats had a good night, but they had a very good night. Absolutely amazed that they won in Texas and places that just seemed like they were really red."

He voted for President Biden in 2020 and President Trump in 2024. In the most recent midterms, he stuck with Republicans despite concerns about the cost of living and the war with Iran.

Gerald in Georgia ran through the list of states where Democrats won senate races in disbelief.

"Come on man, Texas turned blue," Gerald said. "South Carolina turned blue, Ohio, Kansas. Like, this was a referendum of epic proportions."

Gerald is a Biden to Trump voter from Georgia, who has gone all in on MAGA. He's already looking ahead to a future without Trump leading Republicans.

"The Donald Trump era for all intents and purposes is coming to an end in 2028 for certain, if not before that," Gerald said.

Before that, though, Democrats will take power in Washington, at least in part.

Swing Shift voters said again and again when asked about their hopes and fears following these midterms that they hope that the incoming Democratic Congress will focus on the issues that impact their daily lives but fear more of the same broken politics.

"I will choose to hope because that's really all we can do is hope," said Michelle. "Hope that the politicians that were voted in will live up to the promises they made and that change will truly be made."

Even though John didn't vote for Democrats this year, he still wants them to tackle the cost of living.

"Over these next 2 years I hope they are concerned with and concentrate on the affordability issue," John said. "I hope they work with President Trump to try to lower prices. I just hope it's not two years of investigations and impeachment hearings."

item.content:encoded:
ABU DHABI, United Arab Emirates — Officials at U.S.-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine said Wednesday that the sides have agreed a large exchange of prisoners of war.

"One of the positives is we agreed that we're going to have the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners, which we're going to finalize the numbers tomorrow," Jared Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law, said after the two days of talks in Abu Dhabi ended.

Vladimir Medinsky, the head of the Russian delegation, and Rustem Umerov, who led Kyiv's delegation in Abu Dhabi, confirmed the planned exchange.

Hopes were low for any major breakthrough in the first meeting in nine months between the delegations. Russia and Ukraine have from time to time swapped prisoners during their nearly five-year war.

U.S. officials say they are determined to revive Washington's peace efforts that so far have failed to deliver significant results.

Kushner says he and U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff will travel to Moscow on Thursday to meet with President Vladimir Putin, then fly to Dublin to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

The context of the negotiations has changed since the last meeting in February in Geneva. The Trump administration has to reckon with Democrats, who could demand more support for Ukraine, taking over the U.S. Congress in January following the U.S. midterm elections.

Also, Russia's wartime economy is under heavy strain, and Ukraine is reeling from devastating aerial attacks on its power grid.

Umerov said Kyiv's delegation is expected to meet Wednesday with European officials.

Moscow doesn't want European countries, which are concerned about Russia's conduct and broader intentions on the continent, involved in the direct negotiations. However, representatives of European governments, the European Union and NATO were in Abu Dhabi and were consulting with the Ukrainian delegation, officials said.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Tuesday's session was "constructive and quite substantive."

The talks were largely about humanitarian issues, including possible prisoner exchanges and returning Ukrainian civilians in captivity, as well as children taken from the country, he said.

Security guarantees also were discussed, he said. However, Russia and Ukraine have shown no sign of a willingness to compromise on their demands.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the meeting "very productive," while cautioning that a breakthrough on stopping the war will take time.

The Abu Dhabi talks are being held against the backdrop of continued fighting on the front line, where little territory has changed hands this year.

Meanwhile, both countries are battering each other with long-range missiles and drones.

Overnight, Russia struck the southern Zaporizhzhia region and the eastern city of Kharkiv, wounding seven civilians and damaging property.

Russia's Defense Ministry said that air defenses downed 627 Ukrainian drones overnight, 150 of them over the region around St. Petersburg, according to the regional Gov. Alexander Drozdenko.

He said that the drones started a fire at the port of Ust-Luga, one of the main facilities for Russian oil exports, injuring three workers.

item.title: An Iran-backed trio is accused of plotting attacks on a U.K. base hosting U.S. jets

item.content:encoded:
LONDON — Federal prosecutors in New York have charged three men with terrorism offenses over what they describe as an Iran-backed campaign of nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks across Europe and the United States. The charges include a September plot against a British air base where American forces were stationed.

The indictment, unsealed on Tuesday, names Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood Al-Saadi, 32, who holds Iranian and Iraqi citizenship, Mohsen Mohajeri, 48, an Iranian, and Mohammed Ali Al-Hassani, 35, an Iraqi.

Prosecutors allege the men acted on behalf of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and the Iraqi militia Kata'ib Hezbollah to orchestrate, plan and conduct the attacks through a network of associates across Europe and the U.S., targeting Jewish communities and a British base hosting American troops. The indictment cites plots against synagogues in London and in New York. Both Iran's Revolutionary Guard and Kata'ib Hezbollah are designated by the United States as foreign terrorist organizations.

The court filings describe an operation that was directed, in part, by the suspects who were thousands of miles away. In April, prosecutors have alleged, the three men gathered in a room and watched an attack unfold live on a large screen via Apple's FaceTime video calling app. Al-Hassani allegedly coached the attacker through igniting and hurling a series of seemingly incendiary devices while Al-Saadi filmed.

The following day, Al-Hassani is accused of guiding another man on a video call as he lit an improvised explosive and threw it at a synagogue in London.

The men "helped orchestrate a campaign of terror" on behalf of the two designated terror groups, according to U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, Jamie McDonald.

The United Kingdom seems to have been a central target of the plot allegedly perpetrated by the three men: among the roughly 18 attacks claimed last spring by a group calling itself Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya, which prosecutors say was a front for Kata'ib Hezbollah, as many as seven took place in the U.K. It was the most intensely targeted country in Europe, though the indictment does not specify the location of other plots or attacks.

These included arson attacks, the use of explosives, and a near-fatal stabbing of two Jewish men in London — one of whom was a dual U.S.-British citizen.

Prosecutors say that in April the men sat in a room, and directed an attack remotely, in real time, over FaceTime, telling the attacker when to light and throw what seems to have been some kind of incendiary device.

The next day, one of the men, Mohammed Ali Al-Hassani, allegedly told another man attacking a London synagogue to "light it up like a Christmas tree."

According to the indictment, Al-Hassani was operating from Iran, but he began paying associates in Britain in August to film the perimeter of Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford, in Gloucestershire, several hours west of London.

They allegedly obtained vans and drums of fuel, looked into buying chemical accelerants, and gathered metal items that could potentially serve as shrapnel. The vans were fitted with sham branding for a fuel delivery firm as well as a pool supply company.

On Sept. 26, three of these vans had set off toward the base that housed large numbers of U.S. military aircraft. At least two vehicles were stopped at a security roadblock, and British authorities seized all three early the next morning and arrested those inside.

The U.S. almost immediately redeployed several of its long range bombing aircraft from the base at the time of this incident.

The indictment said Al-Saadi had been detained abroad in May and brought to the United States, where prosecutors say he kept directing the network from his jail cell by relaying coded messages through phone calls with relatives in Iraq. He used aliases to refer to his alleged co-conspirators and referred to terrorist activity, including ongoing alleged plots, as "work," while those he spoke to used the phrase "international section" to mean overseas travel, according to the indictment. His sister and mother were among his interlocutors on some of those calls. Three days before the plot, in late September, he allegedly asked them to get money to Al-Hassani for the RAF Fairford operation.

British authorities had earlier charged two men with national security related offenses tied to the incident.

In a separate case, British counterterrorism police said on Tuesday it arrested a 41-year-old member of the U.S. Army on suspicion of offenses under Sections 1 and 3 of Britain's National Security Act 2023.

The suspect, who has not been named by authorities, is a senior U.S. soldier who was stationed at Imjin Barracks near Gloucester, in western England, which is home to NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps, the U.S. Army's Counterintelligence Command told NPR.

Officers have been searching two addresses in the same region of Gloucestershire, to the west of London. The man is being held at a London police station. Police said the allegations concern Russia, and the investigation was "very much ongoing," according to Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator for counterterrorism policing in the U.K.

FBI Director Kash Patel called the arrest important in the context of an uptick in FBI counterintelligence arrest, and said it "involves allegations of espionage" — without giving further details.

"The alleged conduct of a senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent," Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, commanding general of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command, said in a statement to NPR.

Though unrelated, both these cases have occurred in the U.K., a country which hosts a large American military presence. At the start of the war in Iran, Britain's Defense Ministry confirmed to the U.K. Parliament in March that U.S. forces operate eleven RAF bases across the country, with approximately 12,300 American military and civilian defense personnel at various sites.

Responding in January to a written question from a member of Parliament, the ministry said that there were around 11,000 uniformed U.S. personnel in the country, excluding families, civilians and contractors.

The ministry has declined to give figures for individual bases, citing the security of personnel.

The U.S. Air Force's two main operating bases are RAF Lakenheath and RAF Mildenhall in Suffolk, in eastern England. Other sites include RAF Croughton, a communications station in Northamptonshire, and RAF Menwith Hill in North Yorkshire, used primarily by the National Security Agency, according to a House of Commons Library briefing . RAF Fairford serves as a forward operating base for the U.S. Air Force Global Strike Command.

In March, the British government allowed the U.S. to use British bases for limited strikes against missile sites in Iran, according to a parliamentary research service, which identifies Fairford as one of the bases potentially involved.

The threat picture around some U.S. bases seems to have sharpened in recent days. The Wall Street Journal reported , citing people familiar with the matter, that the U.S. military had moved aircraft out of RAF Mildenhall on Monday because of a threat from Iran. NPR did not independently confirm the reports.

Neither the U.K. nor the U.S. government has confirmed the reason for the aircraft movements that have been reported. Britain's Defense Ministry has said aircraft relocate routinely for operational reasons.
